claim: vGluT1 is enriched at PF terminals.

claim: PF synapses (vGluT1+EAAT4+) constituted 88.8% of total synaptosomes.

claim: EPAC can interact with RIM1.

claim: The level of pan-phospho-serine (p-Ser) remained unchanged after 8-pCPT treatment of synaptosomes.

claim: Neither EPAC1 nor EPAC2 altered serine phosphorylation of RIM1α in HEK cells.

claim: Both EPAC1 and EPAC2 increased threonine phosphorylation of RIM1α in HEK cells.

claim: Forskolin increased RIM1 p-Thr in WT synaptosomes.

claim: Co-application of forskolin and ESI-09 did not increase RIM1 p-Thr in WT synaptosomes.
source: RIM1 p-Thr was vastly increased by forskolin alone, but not following co-application of both forskolin and ESI-09 (Figure 1E), indicating that cAMP leads to EPAC-dependent threonine phosphorylation of RIM1.
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: ESI-09 is an inhibitor of EPAC.

evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Gutierrez-Castellanos et al., 2017.

claim: cAMP leads to EPAC-dependent threonine phosphorylation of RIM1.

claim: RIM1 p-Thr was significantly reduced in Rapgef3/4-dKO mice synaptosomes compared to WT.

claim: RIM1 p-Ser was unchanged in Rapgef3/4-dKO mice synaptosomes compared to WT.

claim: Knockout of Rapgef3/4 did not change the expression of RIM1.
source: Meanwhile, knockout of Rapgef3/4 did not change the expression of RIM1 (Figure 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: EPAC deficiency did not interfere with lobule thickness in the cerebellum.
source: The difference of RIM1 p-Thr in the Rapgef3/4-dKO mice was not accompanied by major structural difference, as EPAC deficiency did not interfere with lobule thickness or number of PC spines (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A and B).

claim: EPAC deficiency did not interfere with number of PC spines.
source: The difference of RIM1 p-Thr in the Rapgef3/4-dKO mice was not accompanied by major structural difference, as EPAC deficiency did not interfere with lobule thickness or number of PC spines (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A and B).

claim: EPAC is necessary and sufficient to induce threonine phosphorylation of RIM1.
source: Together, these data strongly indicate that EPAC is necessary and sufficient to induce threonine phosphorylation of RIM1.
evidence: The claim is inferred from multiple experiments showing EPAC activation increases RIM1 p-Thr and EPAC deletion decreases it.

claim: EPAC lacks kinase activity.

claim: PKCε overlapped with vGluT1 in cerebellar synaptosomes.

claim: Phosphorylation at PKCα-S657 or PKCα-T638 was unchanged in Rapgef3/4-dKO versus WT synaptosomes.

claim: RIM1 is critical to organization of the presynaptic active zone.

evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Schoch et al., 2002; Han et al., 2011; Kaeser et al., 2011; Acuna et al., 2016; Persoon et al., 2019.

claim: RIM1 is critical to neurotransmitter release.

claim: No apparent abnormality was found in the synaptic cleft of PF-PC synapses in Rapgef3/4-dKO mice compared to WT.

claim: The total number of vesicles in PF terminals (within 100 nm away from active zone) was not affected by EPAC deletion.

claim: The total number of vesicles in PF terminals was not affected by PKCε deletion in granule cells.

claim: Neither EPAC nor PKCε ablation changed the expression levels of Rab3A and Munc13.

claim: FR236924 is a selective activator of PKCε.

evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 5H and I.

claim: Presynaptic EPAC and PKCε are not required for the induction of postsynaptic forms of LTP and LTD.
source: Overall, our results suggest that presynaptic EPAC and PKCε are not required for the induction of postsynaptic forms of LTP and LTD.
evidence: The claim is inferred from experiments showing postsynaptic LTP and LTD can be induced in mice with presynaptic deletion of EPAC or PKCε.

claim: Basic motor performance was impaired in Rapgef3/4-dKO mice.
source: We found that basic motor performance was impaired in Rapgef3/4-dKO mice in that they showed significant deficits in the amplitude and timing of their OKR (p=0.009 and p=0.004, respectively; ANOVA for repeated measurements) and VOR (p=0.001 and p=0.02, respectively; ANOVA for repeated measurements) (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: Rapgef3/4-dKO mice showed significant deficits in the amplitude and timing of their OKR.
source: We found that basic motor performance was impaired in Rapgef3/4-dKO mice in that they showed significant deficits in the amplitude and timing of their OKR (p=0.009 and p=0.004, respectively; ANOVA for repeated measurements) and VOR (p=0.001 and p=0.02, respectively; ANOVA for repeated measurements) (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Rapgef3/4-dKO mice showed significant deficits in the amplitude and timing of their VOR.

evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B.

claim: No significant differences were observed in the VVOR between Rapgef3/4-dKO and WT mice.
source: In contrast, no significant differences were observed in the VVOR (p=0.66 and p=0.68 for gain and phase values, respectively; Figure 7—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C.

claim: OKR gains of Rapgef3;Rapgef4-cKO mice were significantly lower than those of Atoh1Cre littermates.
source: Basic eye movement performance was also affected in Rapgef3;Rapgef4-cKO mice in that their OKR gains were significantly lower than those of Atoh1Cre littermates (p=0.003; ANOVA for repeated measurements) (Figure 7B), that their VOR gains were significantly greater than those of Atoh1Cre littermates (VOR: p=0.027; ANOVA for repeated measurements) (Figure 7C), and that the phase values during both OKR and VOR were significantly lagging those of the Atoh1Cre littermates (OKR: p=0.001; VOR: p=0.047; ANOVA for repeated measurements) (Figure 7B and C).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: VOR gains of Rapgef3;Rapgef4-cKO mice were significantly greater than those of Atoh1Cre littermates.
source: Basic eye movement performance was also affected in Rapgef3;Rapgef4-cKO mice in that their OKR gains were significantly lower than those of Atoh1Cre littermates (p=0.003; ANOVA for repeated measurements) (Figure 7B), that their VOR gains were significantly greater than those of Atoh1Cre littermates (VOR: p=0.027; ANOVA for repeated measurements) (Figure 7C), and that the phase values during both OKR and VOR were significantly lagging those of the Atoh1Cre littermates (OKR: p=0.001; VOR: p=0.047; ANOVA for repeated measurements) (Figure 7B and C).

claim: The phase values during both OKR and VOR were significantly lagging those of the Atoh1Cre littermates in Rapgef3;Rapgef4-cKO mice.

claim: No significant differences were observed between Rapgef3;Rapgef4-cKO and Atoh1Cre mice in the VVOR.

evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: OKR gain values of Prkce-cKO mice were significantly lower than those of Prkcef/f littermates.
source: Moreover, Prkce-cKO mice shared the same defects with Rapgef3;Rapgef4-cKO mice in their basic motor performance. OKR gain values of Prkce-cKO mice were significantly lower than those of Prkcef/f littermates (p=0.013; ANOVA for repeated measurements) (Figure 7E), whereas their VOR gain values were greater than those of control littermates (p=0.034; ANOVA for repeated measurements) (Figure 7F).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: VOR gain values of Prkce-cKO mice were greater than those of Prkcef/f littermates.

OKR gain values of Prkce-cKO mice were significantly lower than those of Prkcef/f littermates (p=0.013; ANOVA for repeated measurements) (Figure 7E), whereas their VOR gain values were greater than those of control littermates (p=0.034; ANOVA for repeated measurements) (Figure 7F).

claim: No significant differences were observed between Prkcef/f and Prkce-cKO mice in the VVOR.

evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 7G.

claim: Presynaptic ablation of EPAC and/or PKCε mice profoundly influences motor performance when visual and vestibular systems are separated, but not when they are engaged simultaneously.
source: Altogether, our data suggest that presynaptic ablation of EPAC and/or PKCε mice profoundly influences motor performance when visual and vestibular systems are separated, but not when they are engaged simultaneously, as occurs under natural conditions or during visuo-vestibular training.
evidence: The claim is inferred from behavioral data showing deficits in OKR and VOR but not VVOR in EPAC and PKCε knockout mice.

claim: VOR phase reversal aims to reverse the direction of the VOR using retinal slip caused by a screen rotation in the same direction as head rotation.
source: VOR phase reversal aims to reverse the direction of the VOR using retinal slip caused by a screen rotation in the same direction (i.e. in phase) as head rotation and with increasing amplitude as the training progresses (Figure 7H).
evidence: The claim describes the experimental protocol for VOR phase reversal.

claim: All three control mouse lines (WT, Atoh1Cre and Prkcef/f) exhibited gain reductions during initial days of gain-decrease training.
source: During the initial days of gain-decrease training, all three control mouse lines (WT, Atoh1Cre and Prkcef/f) exhibited gain reductions similar to previous work (Wulff et al., 2009; Badura et al., 2016; Gutierrez-Castellanos et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data and is consistent with previous work (Wulff et al., 2009; Badura et al., 2016; Gutierrez-Castellanos et al., 2017).

claim: Gain reductions were smaller in Rapgef3/4-dKO, Rapgef3;Rapgef4-cKO, and Prkce-cKO mice compared to controls.
source: Gain reductions were smaller in Rapgef3/4-dKO (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D), Rapgef3;Rapgef4-cKO (Figure 7I), as well as Prkce-cKO (Figure 7J) mice, but the deficit varied across days between the different mouse lines (in Rapgef3/4-dKO mice, Day 1: p=0.043; Day 2: p=0.008; Day 3: p=0.002; Day 4: p=0.007; Day 5: p=0.004; in Rapgef3;Rapgef4-cKO mice, Day 1: p=0.079; Day 2: p=0.036; Day 3: p=0.011; Day 4: p=0.22; Day 5: p=0.061; and in Prkce-cKO mice, Day 1: p=0.047; Day 2: p=0.004; Day 3: p=0.004; Day 4: p=0.084; Day 5: p=0.15).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1D, Figure 7I, and Figure 7J.

claim: WT, Atoh1Cre, and Prkcef/f mice showed a proper reversal of the phase of their VOR.
source: WT (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D), Atoh1Cre (Figure 7I) as well as Prkcef/f (Figure 7J) mice showed a proper reversal of the phase of their VOR, highlighting their ability to invert the direction of an innate reflex (Wulff et al., 2009; Badura et al., 2016; Peter et al., 2016; Grasselli et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1D, Figure 7I, and Figure 7J, and is consistent with previous work (Wulff et al., 2009; Badura et al., 2016; Peter et al., 2016; Grasselli et al., 2020).

claim: VOR phase values were not significantly affected in the Rapgef3/4-dKO, Rapgef3;Rapgef4-cKO, and Prkce-cKO mouse lines during the first day of VOR phase reversal training.
source: Whereas the VOR phase values were not significantly affected in the Rapgef3/4-dKO, Rapgef3;Rapgef4-cKO, and Prkce-cKO mouse lines during the first day (WT versus Rapgef3/4-dKO, p=0.15; Atoh1Cre versus Rapgef3;Rapgef4-cKO, p=0.087; Prkcef/f versus Prkce-cKO, p=0.52), they were so during sessions on days 2–5 (WT versus Rapgef3/4-dKO: Day 2, p=0.003; Day 3, p=0.002; Day 4, p<0.001; Day 5, p<0.001; Atoh1Cre versus Rapgef3;Rapgef4-cKO: Day 2, p<0.001; Day 3, p<0.001; Day 4, p<0.001; Day 5, p<0.001; Prkcef/f versus Prkce-cKO: Day 2, p=0.01; Day 3, p=0.048; Day 4, p<0.001; Day 5, p<0.001).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1D, Figure 7I, and Figure 7J.

claim: VOR phase values were significantly affected in the Rapgef3/4-dKO, Rapgef3;Rapgef4-cKO, and Prkce-cKO mouse lines during sessions on days 2–5 of VOR phase reversal training.
source: Whereas the VOR phase values were not significantly affected in the Rapgef3/4-dKO, Rapgef3;Rapgef4-cKO, and Prkce-cKO mouse lines during the first day (WT versus Rapgef3/4-dKO, p=0.15; Atoh1Cre versus Rapgef3;Rapgef4-cKO, p=0.087; Prkcef/f versus Prkce-cKO, p=0.52), they were so during sessions on days 2–5 (WT versus Rapgef3/4-dKO: Day 2, p=0.003; Day 3, p=0.002; Day 4, p<0.001; Day 5, p<0.001; Atoh1Cre versus Rapgef3;Rapgef4-cKO: Day 2, p<0.001; Day 3, p<0.001; Day 4, p<0.001; Day 5, p<0.001; Prkcef/f versus Prkce-cKO: Day 2, p=0.01; Day 3, p=0.048; Day 4, p<0.001; Day 5, p<0.001).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1D, Figure 7I, and Figure 7J.

claim: Rapgef3/4-dKO, Rapgef3;Rapgef4-cKO and Prkce-cKO mice had prominent deficits in phase-reversal learning of their VOR.
source: Therefore, we conclude that Rapgef3/4-dKO, Rapgef3;Rapgef4-cKO and Prkce-cKO mice had prominent deficits in phase-reversal learning of their VOR.
evidence: The claim is inferred from behavioral data showing impaired VOR phase reversal in EPAC and PKCε knockout mice.

claim: The EPAC-PKCε module has a critical role in a presynaptic form of long-term potentiation in the cerebellum.
source: Here, we report that the EPAC-PKCε module has a critical role in a presynaptic form of long-term potentiation in the cerebellum and motor behavior in mice.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple experiments showing EPAC-PKCε module is required for presynaptic LTP.

claim: The EPAC-PKCε module has a critical role in motor behavior in mice.
source: Here, we report that the EPAC-PKCε module has a critical role in a presynaptic form of long-term potentiation in the cerebellum and motor behavior in mice.
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral experiments showing motor deficits in EPAC and PKCε knockout mice.

claim: Presynaptic cAMP−EPAC−PKCε signaling cascade induces a previously unidentified threonine phosphorylation of RIM1α.
source: Presynaptic cAMP−EPAC−PKCε signaling cascade induces a previously unidentified threonine phosphorylation of RIM1α, and thereby initiates the assembly of the Rab3A−RIM1α−Munc13-1 tripartite complex that facilitates docking and release of synaptic vesicles.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple experiments showing EPAC-PKCε module induces RIM1α threonine phosphorylation.

claim: Threonine phosphorylation of RIM1α initiates the assembly of the Rab3A−RIM1α−Munc13-1 tripartite complex that facilitates docking and release of synaptic vesicles.
source: Presynaptic cAMP−EPAC−PKCε signaling cascade induces a previously unidentified threonine phosphorylation of RIM1α, and thereby initiates the assembly of the Rab3A−RIM1α−Munc13-1 tripartite complex that facilitates docking and release of synaptic vesicles.
evidence: The claim is inferred from experiments showing RIM1α phosphorylation increases binding to Rab3A and Munc13-1, and increases vesicle docking and release.

claim: Granule cell-specific blocking of EPAC−PKCε signaling abolishes presynaptic long-term potentiation at the parallel fiber to Purkinje cell synapses.
source: Granule cell-specific blocking of EPAC−PKCε signaling abolishes presynaptic long-term potentiation at the parallel fiber to Purkinje cell synapses and impairs basic performance and learning of cerebellar motor behavior.
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology experiments showing presynaptic LTP is blocked in mice with granule cell-specific deletion of EPAC or PKCε.

claim: Granule cell-specific blocking of EPAC−PKCε signaling impairs basic performance and learning of cerebellar motor behavior.
source: Granule cell-specific blocking of EPAC−PKCε signaling abolishes presynaptic long-term potentiation at the parallel fiber to Purkinje cell synapses and impairs basic performance and learning of cerebellar motor behavior.

claim: Presynaptic plasticity is regulated through a novel signaling cascade involving EPAC-PKCε.
source: These results unveil a functional relevance of presynaptic plasticity that is regulated through a novel signaling cascade, thereby enriching the spectrum of cerebellar learning mechanisms.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the discovery of the EPAC-PKCε-RIM1α signaling cascade regulating presynaptic LTP.

claim: The EPAC-PKCε signaling cascade enriches the spectrum of cerebellar learning mechanisms.
